briefing: Shortly after Israel's victories at Jericho and Ai, a group of weary strangers arrives at Joshua's camp in Gilgal. They carry worn-out sacks, patched wineskins and dry, mouldy bread, and they ask for a peace treaty. Investigate Joshua 9 to find out who these travellers really are and what happened.

stages.clue: Camp report: the visitors' sacks are old, their wine bottles torn and bound up, their shoes patched, and all their bread dry and mouldy. Word has it they had heard what Joshua did to Jericho and Ai.
stages.prompt: According to the text, the inhabitants of which town planned this disguise?
options: Gibeon
Jericho
Ai
Gilgal
stages.explanation: Joshua 9:3-5 says the inhabitants of Gibeon 'did work wilily' and came with old sacks, old shoes and mouldy bread. Jericho and Ai were the cities Joshua had already conquered, and Gilgal was Israel's camp (Joshua 9:6).
stages.hint: The plotters had heard about Jericho and Ai, so they were not from either of those cities.

stages.clue: Witness statement: one of the travellers held up a piece of dry bread and told the Israelites a story about when it had been packed.
stages.prompt: What did the travellers claim about their bread?
options: They took it hot out of their houses on the day they set out
They bought it at a market in Gilgal
They received it as a gift from the king of Ai
They baked it fresh that morning
stages.explanation: In Joshua 9:12-13 the travellers said they took the bread hot from their houses when they set out, and that it had become dry and mouldy, their bottles torn and clothes worn 'by reason of the very long journey.'
stages.hint: They used the bread to suggest how long they had been travelling.

stages.clue: Procedure note: the Israelite men examined the visitors' food, and Joshua and the princes swore an oath of peace. One important step was left out.
stages.prompt: What did the men of Israel fail to do before making the league?
options: They asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD
They did not taste the visitors' food
They did not let the princes swear
They did not let Joshua make peace
stages.explanation: Joshua 9:14 says the men took of their victuals 'and asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD.' Verse 15 shows Joshua made peace and the princes swore, so the other options contradict the text.
stages.hint: They checked the evidence with their own eyes but did not seek guidance from someone else.

stages.clue: Follow-up report: just three days after the treaty, Israel received news about the strangers and marched to their cities, arriving on the third day.
stages.prompt: What did Israel discover about the travellers?
options: They were neighbours who dwelt among them
They lived beyond the great sea
They came from Egypt
They were Israelites from another tribe
stages.explanation: Joshua 9:16 says Israel heard 'that they were their neighbours, and that they dwelt among them,' and verse 17 names their cities: Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth and Kirjathjearim.
stages.hint: The 'very long journey' turned out to be much shorter than claimed.

stages.clue: Final interrogation: Joshua asked, 'Wherefore have ye beguiled us?' The Gibeonites gave their reason and placed themselves in his hand.
stages.prompt: Case solved: what really happened, and how did it end?
options: The Gibeonites, sore afraid for their lives, pretended to come from far away; they were spared but made hewers of wood and drawers of water
The Gibeonites were truly from a far country and became Israel's honoured allies
The men of Ai disguised themselves, and Joshua destroyed them
The Gibeonites stole Israel's bread and were driven out of the land
stages.explanation: In Joshua 9:24 the Gibeonites said they 'were sore afraid of our lives' and so 'have done this thing.' Joshua 9:26-27 says he delivered them from being slain and made them hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and the altar of the LORD.
stages.hint: Their lives were spared because of the oath, but their deception had a lasting consequence.

briefing: A man known to have been blind from birth is suddenly seen walking the streets with full sight, and his neighbors cannot agree whether he is even the same man. The religious leaders open an inquiry, questioning the man and his parents. Reconstruct what really happened from the case file of John 9.

stages.clue: Witness report: Jesus and his disciples passed a man blind since birth, and the disciples asked their Master a pointed question about blame.
stages.prompt: According to Jesus, why was this man born blind?
options: Because his parents had sinned
Because the man himself had sinned
So that the works of God should be made manifest in him
Because he had broken the sabbath
stages.explanation: Jesus answered that neither the man nor his parents had sinned, but that the works of God should be made manifest in him (John 9:3).
stages.hint: Jesus rejected both options the disciples suggested.

stages.clue: Physical evidence: traces of clay made with spittle were applied to the man's eyes, and he was given instructions to go somewhere.
stages.prompt: Where was the man told to go and wash?
options: The river Jordan
The pool of Siloam
The pool of Bethesda
The temple laver
stages.explanation: Jesus anointed the man's eyes with clay and told him, 'Go, wash in the pool of Siloam'; he washed and came seeing (John 9:6-7).
stages.hint: The name of this pool is interpreted as 'Sent.'

stages.clue: Pharisee testimony: 'This man is not of God,' some of them said of the healer, pointing to the day on which the clay was made.
stages.prompt: On what day did Jesus make the clay and open the man's eyes?
options: The day of Pentecost
The first day of the week
The sabbath day
The day of atonement
stages.explanation: It was the sabbath day when Jesus made the clay, and some Pharisees said he was not of God because he kept not the sabbath day (John 9:14,16).
stages.hint: Their objection concerned a weekly day of rest.

stages.clue: Statement of the parents: 'We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind... he is of age; ask him.'
stages.prompt: Why did the man's parents refuse to say how their son received his sight?
options: They feared the Jews, who had agreed to put out of the synagogue anyone who confessed Jesus was Christ
They had not seen their son in many years
They believed he had been healed by a physician
They were angry with their son
stages.explanation: His parents spoke this way because they feared the Jews, who had agreed that anyone confessing Jesus as Christ would be put out of the synagogue (John 9:22).
stages.hint: Consider what the text says would happen to anyone who made a certain confession.

stages.clue: Final report: after the man was cast out, Jesus found him and asked, 'Dost thou believe on the Son of God?'
stages.prompt: What really happened when Jesus revealed himself to the healed man?
options: The man went away doubting
The man returned to the Pharisees to accuse Jesus
The man said, 'Lord, I believe,' and worshipped him
The man asked for another sign before believing
stages.explanation: When Jesus said, 'it is he that talketh with thee,' the man replied, 'Lord, I believe,' and he worshipped him (John 9:37-38).
stages.hint: The man's answer was short and his response was immediate.

briefing: Case File: The Stolen Blessing. In Genesis 27, an aged Isaac prepares to bless his son before he dies, yet the blessing ends up in unexpected hands. Examine the evidence in Genesis 27 to reconstruct exactly what happened in Isaac's tent.

stages.clue: Witness report: The patriarch is old and his eyes are dim. He was heard sending his elder son out to the field with quiver and bow, promising a blessing afterward.
stages.prompt: What did Isaac ask Esau to bring him before giving the blessing?
options: Venison made into savoury meat
A lamb from the flock for a sacrifice
Bread and wine from the city
Water from a well in the wilderness
stages.explanation: Isaac told Esau to take his weapons, hunt venison, and make savoury meat, 'that my soul may bless thee before I die' (Genesis 27:3-4).
stages.hint: Think of what a hunter brings home from the field.

stages.clue: Overheard conversation: Someone in the household heard Isaac's instructions to Esau and quickly gave Jacob a set of instructions of her own.
stages.prompt: What did Rebekah tell Jacob to fetch from the flock?
options: Two good kids of the goats
A young bullock
Seven ewe lambs
A pair of turtledoves
keywords: two good kids of the goats
stages.explanation: Rebekah told Jacob to fetch 'two good kids of the goats' so she could make savoury meat for Isaac (Genesis 27:9).
stages.hint: The animals came from the flock and their skins would prove useful later.

stages.clue: Physical evidence: Jacob had worried that his father would feel him, since his brother was hairy and he was smooth. The garments and some animal skins were later found to have been used.
stages.prompt: How was Jacob disguised before going in to Isaac?
options: He wore Esau's goodly raiment and goat skins on his hands and neck
He wore a veil over his face
He covered himself with sackcloth and ashes
He wore a priest's linen ephod
stages.explanation: Rebekah put Esau's goodly raiment on Jacob and put the skins of the kids of the goats on his hands and the smooth of his neck (Genesis 27:15-16).
stages.hint: The disguise targeted Isaac's sense of touch and borrowed from the elder brother's wardrobe.

stages.clue: Statement from the tent: After feeling his son, the blind father voiced a doubt about what he heard compared with what he felt.
stages.prompt: What did Isaac say when he felt Jacob?
options: The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau
The smell is not the smell of my son
Thou art too young to be Esau
Thy meat is not as I love it
stages.explanation: Isaac felt him and said, 'The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau,' and he discerned him not (Genesis 27:22-23).
stages.hint: One sense told Isaac the truth while another was deceived.

stages.clue: Final testimony: When the true elder son arrived from hunting, Isaac trembled very exceedingly and explained to him what had happened.
stages.prompt: According to Isaac's explanation to Esau, who had taken the blessing?
options: Jacob, his brother, who came with subtilty
A servant who stole Esau's garments
Rebekah, who asked for it herself
No one; Isaac had not yet blessed anyone
stages.explanation: Isaac told Esau, 'Thy brother came with subtilty, and hath taken away thy blessing' (Genesis 27:35).
stages.hint: Isaac named the culprit by his relation to Esau.

briefing: After being healed of leprosy, the Syrian captain Naaman returns to the man of God with gifts and then sets off for home. Soon afterward silver and garments change hands on the road, and a servant's story does not match the facts. Examine 2 Kings 5:15-27 to uncover what happened on this secret errand.

stages.clue: Witness statement from Naaman's company: 'Our master stood before the prophet and begged him to accept a gift. The prophet swore an oath by the LORD and would not budge.'
stages.prompt: How did Elisha respond when Naaman urged him to take a blessing (a gift)?
options: He refused, saying, 'As the LORD liveth, before whom I stand, I will receive none.'
He accepted half of the gift for the sons of the prophets.
He told Naaman to send the gift to the king of Israel.
He accepted only the changes of garments.
stages.explanation: Naaman asked Elisha to take a blessing, but Elisha swore he would receive none and refused even when urged (2 Kings 5:15-16).
stages.hint: Pay attention to the oath the prophet swore.

stages.clue: Report from the road: 'A man came running after the chariot. Naaman stepped down to meet him and asked, Is all well? The runner said his master had sent him.'
stages.prompt: What reason did Gehazi give Naaman for coming after him?
options: Elisha had changed his mind and wanted the whole gift.
Two young men of the sons of the prophets had come from mount Ephraim and needed a talent of silver and two changes of garments.
The king of Israel demanded payment for the healing.
Naaman had left his mules' burden of earth behind.
stages.explanation: Gehazi claimed his master had sent him because two young men of the sons of the prophets had arrived from mount Ephraim, and he asked for a talent of silver and two changes of garments (2 Kings 5:22).
stages.hint: The runner mentioned visitors from a hill country region.

stages.clue: Inventory note: 'Bound in two bags and carried by two of Naaman's servants, along with two changes of garments.'
stages.prompt: How much silver did Naaman actually give?
options: One talent of silver
Ten talents of silver
Two talents of silver
Six thousand pieces of gold
stages.explanation: Naaman said, 'Be content, take two talents,' and bound two talents of silver in two bags with two changes of garments (2 Kings 5:23).
stages.hint: Naaman gave more than was requested; count the bags.

stages.clue: Observation near the hill: 'Two Syrian servants carried bags ahead of the man, then were sent away empty-handed. The goods were not seen again.'
stages.prompt: What did Gehazi do with the silver and garments when he came to the tower?
options: He gave them to the two young men from mount Ephraim.
He took them from the servants' hands and bestowed them in the house, then let the men go.
He brought them openly to Elisha.
He buried them beside the Jordan.
stages.explanation: At the tower Gehazi took the goods from the servants, bestowed them in the house, and sent the men away (2 Kings 5:24).
stages.hint: Look at where he stopped and where the goods were put.

stages.clue: Final interview: Elisha asked, 'Whence comest thou, Gehazi?' The servant answered that he had gone nowhere, but the prophet said his heart had gone with him.
stages.prompt: What really happened when Gehazi stood before Elisha?
options: Gehazi confessed, and Elisha forgave him without consequence.
Elisha believed Gehazi, and the matter was forgotten.
Gehazi lied, saying 'Thy servant went no whither'; Elisha revealed he knew, and Naaman's leprosy came upon Gehazi.
Naaman returned to reclaim the silver, and Gehazi fled.
stages.explanation: Gehazi claimed he went no whither, but Elisha declared that his heart went with him, and Gehazi left a leper as white as snow (2 Kings 5:25-27).
stages.hint: Compare Gehazi's answer with what Elisha said he already knew.

briefing: A foreign king has ruled Israel for years, until one day he is found dead behind locked doors in his own private chamber, and the visitor who last saw him alive has vanished. Your case file is Judges 3:12-30: follow the evidence from the oppression of Israel to the final outcome, staying strictly with what the text reports.

stages.clue: Background report: Israel did evil in the sight of the LORD, and a foreign ruler allied with Ammon and Amalek seized the city of palm trees.
stages.prompt: Who was the ruler oppressing Israel, and for how long did Israel serve him?
options: Eglon the king of Moab, for eighteen years
Jabin king of Canaan, for twenty years
Eglon the king of Ammon, for seven years
Cushanrishathaim of Mesopotamia, for forty years
stages.explanation: The LORD strengthened Eglon the king of Moab against Israel, and the children of Israel served him eighteen years (Judges 3:12-14).
stages.hint: Ammon and Amalek were his allies, not his own kingdom.

stages.clue: Suspect profile: a Benjamite, the son of Gera, sent by Israel to carry a present to the king. He prepared a weapon before the journey.
stages.prompt: Where did Ehud conceal the two-edged dagger he made?
options: Under his raiment upon his left thigh
Inside the present carried to the king
Under his raiment upon his right thigh
In the sleeve of his left arm
stages.explanation: Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite, made a two-edged dagger a cubit long and girded it under his raiment upon his right thigh (Judges 3:15-16).
stages.hint: Think about which side a left-handed man would draw from.

stages.clue: Witness statement: after the present was delivered and the bearers sent away, the messenger turned back from the quarries by Gilgal and asked to see the king privately.
stages.prompt: What did Ehud say to Eglon once they were alone in the summer parlour?
options: I bring tribute from the elders of Israel
I have a message from God unto thee
I come to swear peace between our peoples
I have a letter from the king of Ammon
stages.explanation: Ehud first claimed a secret errand so the attendants went out, then in the summer parlour said, 'I have a message from God unto thee,' and Eglon arose from his seat (Judges 3:19-20).
stages.hint: The king rose from his seat when he heard who the message was from.

stages.clue: Scene report: the visitor left through the porch. Afterward the king's servants waited a long time outside the parlour before anyone went in.
stages.prompt: According to the text, why did the servants delay entering the parlour?
options: Ehud had ordered them to stay outside until evening
They feared the king's anger at being disturbed at a feast
The doors were locked, and they supposed he covereth his feet in his summer chamber
They could not find anyone to open the doors until morning
stages.explanation: Finding the parlour doors locked, the servants said, 'Surely he covereth his feet in his summer chamber,' and tarried until they were ashamed, then used a key and found their lord dead (Judges 3:24-25).
stages.hint: The locked doors led them to assume the king wanted privacy.

stages.clue: Final report: while the servants tarried, the messenger was already gone. A trumpet was soon heard in the mountain of Ephraim.
stages.prompt: What was the outcome of the case after Ehud escaped?
options: Ehud escaped unto Seirath, Israel took the fords of Jordan, Moab was subdued, and the land had rest fourscore years
Ehud was captured at the quarries, but Israel later defeated Moab and had rest forty years
Ehud fled to Gilgal, Moab's army escaped across the Jordan, and the land had rest twenty years
Ehud became king over Israel and made peace with Moab for eighty years
stages.explanation: Ehud escaped unto Seirath, rallied Israel, seized the fords of Jordan so no Moabite passed over, and Moab was subdued; the land had rest fourscore years (Judges 3:26-30).
stages.hint: Watch the fords of Jordan, and note how many years of rest 'fourscore' means.

briefing: In Jezreel, a man named Naboth is dead and his vineyard has a new owner. Your task is to work through the record of 1 Kings 21 and establish who wanted the land, why it was refused, how Naboth was condemned, and what the LORD declared about it.

stages.clue: Surveyor's note: The vineyard in question lay in Jezreel, right beside the palace of Ahab king of Samaria. The king made an offer for it.
stages.prompt: According to Ahab's offer, what did he want to turn Naboth's vineyard into?
options: A garden of herbs
A courtyard for his chariots
A burial ground for his fathers
A threshing floor for grain
stages.explanation: Ahab asked for the vineyard 'that I may have it for a garden of herbs, because it is near unto my house,' offering a better vineyard or its worth in money (1 Kings 21:2).
stages.hint: Ahab said he wanted it because it was near his house. Look at what kind of garden he named.

stages.clue: Witness statement: The king came home heavy and displeased, lay on his bed, turned his face away and would eat no bread, all because of Naboth's answer.
stages.prompt: What reason did Naboth give for refusing to give up his vineyard?
options: The price Ahab offered was too low
It was the inheritance of his fathers
He had already promised it to Jezebel
The vines were about to be harvested
stages.explanation: Naboth said, 'The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee,' and Ahab went home heavy and displeased (1 Kings 21:3-4).
stages.hint: Naboth's answer was about family land, not about money.

stages.clue: Exhibit A: Letters were delivered to the elders and nobles of Naboth's city. They bore the king's name and were sealed with the king's seal.
stages.prompt: Who actually wrote the letters sent in Ahab's name?
options: Ahab himself
The elders of Jezreel
Jezebel
Elijah the Tishbite
stages.explanation: After promising Ahab, 'I will give thee the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite,' Jezebel 'wrote letters in Ahab's name, and sealed them with his seal' (1 Kings 21:7-8).
stages.hint: Look for the person who told Ahab to arise, eat bread, and let his heart be merry.

stages.clue: Court record: A fast was proclaimed and Naboth was set on high among the people. Two men sat before him and testified in public.
stages.prompt: What accusation did the two men of Belial bring against Naboth?
options: That he had stolen from the king's treasury
That he had moved his neighbour's landmark
That he had worshipped Baal
That he did blaspheme God and the king
stages.explanation: The men of Belial witnessed, 'Naboth did blaspheme God and the king,' and he was carried out of the city and stoned until he died (1 Kings 21:13).
stages.hint: The letters scripted the exact charge in advance. Compare the instruction with the testimony.

stages.clue: Final report: As Ahab went down to take possession of the vineyard, the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite with a question for the king.
stages.prompt: In the LORD's message through Elijah, what did He charge Ahab with?
options: Having killed, and also taken possession
Only failing to pay a fair price for the land
Breaking a treaty with the king of Syria
Refusing to proclaim a fast
stages.explanation: The LORD sent Elijah to say, 'Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?' and declared that dogs would lick Ahab's blood where they licked Naboth's (1 Kings 21:19).
stages.hint: The LORD's question named two things together: what happened to Naboth and what happened to the vineyard.

briefing: A sealed and guarded tomb in Jerusalem was found open, and a story soon spread that the body had been stolen in the night. Your task is to trace the guards' account from the setting of the watch to the report that went around the city, using Matthew 27:62-66 and Matthew 28:1-15. Follow the evidence in order and let the text decide.

stages.clue: Case file, day after the preparation: a delegation met the governor. One of them was recorded saying, 'Sir, we remember that that deceiver said... After three days I will rise again.'
stages.prompt: Who went to Pilate, and what did they say they feared?
options: The chief priests and Pharisees, fearing the disciples would steal the body and say he was risen
The disciples, fearing the Romans would move the body
Joseph of Arimathaea, fearing robbers would damage the tomb
The elders of Galilee, fearing a riot at the feast
stages.explanation: The chief priests and Pharisees came to Pilate asking that the sepulchre be made sure, 'lest his disciples come by night, and steal him away' (Matthew 27:62-64).
stages.hint: Look at who 'came together unto Pilate' and the phrase beginning 'lest his disciples...'

stages.clue: Governor's reply on record: 'Ye have a watch: go your way, make it as sure as ye can.' A later inspection noted marks on the stone.
stages.prompt: What two measures were taken to secure the sepulchre?
options: The stone was sealed and a watch was set
The door was bricked up and the key given to Pilate
The body was moved and the tomb left empty
A second stone was added and the disciples were arrested
stages.explanation: They went and made the sepulchre sure, 'sealing the stone, and setting a watch' (Matthew 27:65-66).
stages.hint: The final verse names two actions joined by 'and'.

stages.clue: Early on the first day of the week, two women came to see the sepulchre. Witnesses felt the ground shake, and the stone was no longer in the door.
stages.prompt: According to the text, who rolled back the stone, and what happened to the keepers?
options: The angel of the Lord rolled it back, and the keepers shook and became as dead men
The disciples rolled it back while the keepers slept
The women rolled it back, and the keepers fled to Pilate
The earthquake moved it, and the keepers arrested the women
stages.explanation: The angel of the Lord descended, rolled back the stone and sat upon it, and 'for fear of him the keepers did shake, and became as dead men' (Matthew 28:2-4).
stages.hint: Check who 'descended from heaven' and how the keepers reacted 'for fear of him'.

stages.clue: Statement attributed to the figure at the tomb, addressed to the women: 'Fear not ye.' He then invited them to look at a certain place.
stages.prompt: What did the angel tell the women about Jesus?
options: He is not here, for he is risen, as he said
His body had been taken to another tomb
The guards had hidden him in the city
He would remain in the tomb until the fourth day
stages.explanation: The angel said, 'He is not here: for he is risen, as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord lay' (Matthew 28:6).
stages.hint: The angel connects his words to what Jesus himself had said earlier.

stages.clue: Final report: some of the watch went into the city and told the chief priests all that was done. Soon afterward a particular saying was 'commonly reported among the Jews.'
stages.prompt: Case solved: where did the story that the disciples stole the body come from?
options: The chief priests and elders gave the soldiers large money to say the disciples stole him while they slept
The soldiers personally saw the disciples carry the body away
The women told the disciples that the body had been stolen
Pilate announced it after investigating the tomb himself
keywords: stole him away while we slept
stages.explanation: After taking counsel, the chief priests and elders 'gave large money unto the soldiers,' telling them to say 'His disciples came by night, and stole him away while we slept,' and the soldiers 'did as they were taught' (Matthew 28:12-15).
stages.hint: Notice who paid whom, and the phrase 'did as they were taught'.

briefing: A riot has shaken the city of Ephesus, and a crowd has packed the theatre shouting the name of a goddess. Your assignment is to reconstruct what happened from the case file in Acts 19:23-41: who stirred the trouble, why, where it spread, and how it ended. Stay with the record; the text alone is your evidence.

stages.clue: Trade ledger note: a local craftsman known for making small silver shrines for Diana is said to have brought 'no small gain' to the craftsmen of the city. He called a meeting of his fellow workmen.
stages.prompt: Who called the craftsmen together at the start of the uproar, and what was his trade?
options: Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines for Diana
Alexander, a coppersmith who made idols for Jupiter
Gaius, a tentmaker who sold goods in the market
The townclerk, a scribe who kept the temple records
stages.explanation: Acts 19:24-25 names Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines for Diana, as the man who called together the workmen of like occupation.
stages.hint: Look for the man whose craft brought 'no small gain unto the craftsmen.'

stages.clue: Witness statement from the craftsmen's meeting: 'He told us that by this craft we have our wealth, and that one man had turned away much people, not only at Ephesus but almost throughout all Asia.'
stages.prompt: According to the speech at the meeting, what was Paul saying that put the craft in danger?
options: That the temple of Diana should be torn down by force
That they be no gods, which are made with hands
That the craftsmen were charging unfair prices
That the shrines should be given away rather than sold
stages.explanation: In Acts 19:26-27 the speaker says Paul persuaded many, saying 'they be no gods, which are made with hands,' so that 'this our craft is in danger to be set at nought' and Diana's temple would be despised.
stages.hint: The complaint concerns what is fashioned by human hands.

stages.clue: Scene report: the whole city was filled with confusion. Two of Paul's travel companions from Macedonia were seized, and the crowd rushed with one accord to a public gathering place. Paul's friends urged him not to go in.
stages.prompt: Where did the crowd rush, and whom did they seize?
options: Into the temple of Diana, seizing Paul and Silas
Into the synagogue, seizing Alexander and Demetrius
Into the theatre, seizing Gaius and Aristarchus
Into the marketplace, seizing Timothy and Erastus
stages.explanation: Acts 19:29 records that the crowd caught Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, and rushed into the theatre; verses 30-31 add that the disciples and certain of the chief of Asia kept Paul from entering.
stages.hint: Paul's friends begged him not to 'adventure himself' into this place.

stages.clue: Crowd observer's note: 'Some cried one thing, and some another; most did not even know why they had come. A man was put forward to speak and beckoned with his hand, but the moment they learned who he was, they drowned him out.'
stages.prompt: What happened when Alexander tried to make his defence to the people?
options: The crowd listened quietly and then went home
When they knew he was a Jew, they cried out for about two hours, 'Great is Diana of the Ephesians'
Demetrius answered him and the two debated for an hour
He was immediately arrested by the deputies
keywords: Great is Diana of the Ephesians
stages.explanation: Acts 19:33-34 says Alexander beckoned to make his defence, but when the crowd knew he was a Jew, all with one voice cried out for about the space of two hours, 'Great is Diana of the Ephesians.'
stages.hint: Count how long the single chant went on.

stages.clue: Final entry: a city official finally quieted the crowd. He pointed out that the accused men were neither robbers of churches nor blasphemers of the goddess, that the courts were open, and that the city itself risked being called to account for the day's uproar.
stages.prompt: Case solution: who ended the uproar, and how was it resolved?
options: Paul entered the theatre and persuaded the crowd to disperse
Demetrius withdrew his complaint and apologized to the city
The townclerk appeased the people, directed complaints to the law and lawful assembly, and dismissed the assembly
Roman soldiers broke up the crowd and imprisoned Gaius and Aristarchus
stages.explanation: Acts 19:35-41 records that the townclerk appeased the people, said any matter should go to the law, the deputies, or a lawful assembly, warned of being called in question for the uproar, and then dismissed the assembly.
stages.hint: The resolution came from a city official, not from Paul or the craftsmen.

briefing: In Jerusalem, a band of men has sworn a deadly oath against the apostle Paul, who is being held by the Roman chief captain. Your assignment is to trace the conspiracy from its first vow to its final outcome, using only the evidence recorded in Acts 23:12-35.

stages.clue: Case note: At daybreak a group gathered and bound themselves under a curse. Their number was counted at more than forty.
stages.prompt: What did the conspirators vow they would not do until they had killed Paul?
options: Neither eat nor drink
Neither sleep nor rest
Neither enter the temple nor pray
Neither leave Jerusalem nor speak to anyone
stages.explanation: Acts 23:12 says they bound themselves under a curse, "saying that they would neither eat nor drink till they had killed Paul," and verse 13 says they were more than forty.
stages.hint: Their oath concerned their daily needs at the table.

stages.clue: Overheard plan: The conspirators went to certain leaders and asked them to pass a request to the chief captain, so Paul would be brought out of the castle.
stages.prompt: What pretext were the leaders to use for having Paul brought down to the council?
options: That Paul had asked to make a public defense
As though they would enquire something more perfectly concerning him
That Paul was to be released to his family
That Paul was to be sent to Rome for trial
stages.explanation: In Acts 23:15 the conspirators told the chief priests and elders to ask that Paul be brought down "as though ye would enquire something more perfectly concerning him," while they waited to kill him before he came near.
stages.hint: The cover story pretended the council wanted more information.

stages.clue: Witness report: A young man entered the castle and told Paul about the men lying in wait. Paul then had a centurion bring him to the chief captain.
stages.prompt: Who was the young man who brought word of the ambush?
options: One of the centurions
A servant of the high priest
Paul's sister's son
One of the forty conspirators
stages.explanation: Acts 23:16 says that "when Paul's sister's son heard of their lying in wait, he went and entered into the castle, and told Paul," and he later repeated the warning to the chief captain privately.
stages.hint: He was a relative of Paul.

stages.clue: Military order: Two centurions were told to make ready two hundred soldiers, threescore and ten horsemen, and two hundred spearmen at the third hour of the night, with beasts provided for Paul.
stages.prompt: Where, and to whom, was Paul to be brought safely?
options: To Rome, to Caesar
To Damascus, to the governor of the city
To Antioch, to the church elders
To Caesarea, to Felix the governor
stages.explanation: Acts 23:23-24 records the order to go to Caesarea and "bring him safe unto Felix the governor."
stages.hint: The destination was a coastal city where a Roman governor sat.

stages.clue: Final report: The soldiers took Paul by night, the horsemen went on with him, and a letter was delivered to the governor along with the prisoner.
stages.prompt: What really happened to Paul after the plot was exposed?
options: He was brought by night to Antipatris, then to Caesarea, and the governor had him kept in Herod's judgment hall until his accusers came
He was handed back to the council, who released him after questioning
He escaped the soldiers and fled to Cilicia
He was killed on the road before reaching the governor
stages.explanation: Acts 23:31-33 says the soldiers brought Paul by night to Antipatris and then presented him to the governor at Caesarea, and verse 35 says the governor would hear him when his accusers came and commanded him to be kept in Herod's judgment hall.
stages.hint: The plot failed, but Paul remained in custody awaiting a hearing.
